+**Status:** Draft v1 · **Source of truth for requirements:** `docs/ProductSpec/Coding_Agent_Economics.md`

+## 1. Purpose and Scope
+This document describes the architecture of the platform that collects coding-agent usage
+data from developer machines, turns it into cost / productivity / quality intelligence, and
+presents it to engineering leadership (Enterprise and Team plans) and, later, to individual
+developers.
+**In scope for this design (Release 1):**
+- Collect session data from **Claude Code** and **Codex** (both write local JSONL files) and
+  **Cursor** (writes to a local SQLite database), *while the session is in progress* — not
+  after it ends.
+- Normalize everything into one common schema so every downstream feature is
+  agent-vendor-neutral.
+- Compute per-session metrics: cost, model mix, tokens, cache efficiency, sub-agents, tools,
+  files changed (Spec RQ-01).
+- Correlate sessions with git activity for productivity measures (Spec RQ-02).
+- Serve an enterprise dashboard and query API with org / team / user tenancy.
+- Batch (after-the-fact) processing of JSONL files as a **side goal** — same pipeline, different feeder.
+**Deliberately deferred, but the architecture leaves room for:**
+- Task classification and session quality scoring (Spec RQ-03, RQ-04) — the pipeline has a
+  slot for it (§5.4), but it is not needed for the first release to work.
+- Governance and realtime control (gateway integration, quotas, kill/throttle) — Phase 2.
+- Dev-local personal view (privacy-preserving, laptop-only).
+**Guiding principles** (from the product brief):
+1. **Simple first, decomposable later.** Fewest moving parts that still have clean seams. Every
+   seam is an interface (§6) so a piece can be pulled out into its own service when scale demands.

+**How it works.** Arriving events are ordinary rows in the events table, each carrying a
+processed-marker, in arrival order. A worker claims work by asking the database for the next
+batch of unprocessed rows and locking them in the same statement; Postgres's "skip locked"
+behavior means a second worker asking at the same moment does not wait on those locked rows —
+it is handed the *next* unlocked batch instead. That one behavior is the whole queue: no
+broker, no polling coordination, no duplicate hand-out between concurrent workers. The worker
+processes its batch and, in a single transaction, writes its results and marks the rows
+processed. If a worker crashes mid-batch, its transaction never commits, its locks vanish
+with its connection, and the rows automatically return to the pool — crash recovery needs no
+visibility timeouts, heartbeats, or requeue logic. Two details keep it fast as the table
+grows: a partial index covering only unprocessed rows, so the claim query never scans the
+processed bulk; and queue-depth monitoring that is a plain row count. Per-session ordering is
+preserved by claiming sessions, not individual events (§5.3).
